analysis: The broad option includes literary genres, world literature, myth, memoir, adaptation and criticism. Rhetoric, stylistics and psycholinguistics give sustained attention to meaning and language, while modern history, sociology and media ground cultural interpretation. Qualitative methods and evidence synthesis supply tools for research. The plan does not reproduce the English grammar, phonology or history sequence.

The adaptation option foregrounds literary form, myth, art and film. Renaissance visual and cross-cultural study and the history of empires support historically informed interpretation. The selection includes close reading, media history, comparative literary theory and documentary production. These are stronger complements for literary reception than general statistics or sociology alone.

The language and public culture option foregrounds rhetoric, stylistics, psycholinguistics, attention and memory, social cognition and discourse. Sociology, the history of empires and Native American histories connect identity and representation to institutions and colonial histories. The shared literary and visual subjects provide concrete cases. This option supports the language-use and identity interests with narrower coverage of historical and regional varieties of English.

The plans differ by 52.5, 45 and 67.5 EC each way. Psycholinguistics is now in its first available spring, after the required brain-and-behaviour course. The comparison identifies selected literature, stylistics and rhetoric correspondences and leaves the dedicated English linguistics and literary-period requirements distinct. The thesis and research seminar remain separate from optional independent research.
constructionStop: Three coherent, distinct options reach the programme limit.

HCBCOGN312.contribution: studies human language processing and acquisition through cognitive and neurological evidence
HCBCOGN312.topics: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
